newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions to fight for health care control.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions to fight for health care control.

text.p: Argentine unions Tuesday vowed to fight President Carlos Menem's decree that would end their control over employee health care plans.
"We totally reject it," Rodolfo Daer, head of the main union federation CGT, told reporters. "The central issue, workers' health, is not being taken into account."
He said the CGT secretariat will meet Wednesday to discuss how best to respond to Menem's decree signed late Monday.
And Lorenzo Miguel, leader of the powerful metalworkers union, warned Menem: "I don't know if the president is strong enough to take on the Argentine labor movement, which has always triumphed."
The decree would allow workers to choose from any union plan as of next January, ending the undisputed control that President Juan Peron gave labor in the 1950s.
But Menem, a Peronist, has departed from Peron's populist style and adopted market policies which have led to clashes with unionized workers, the party's traditional allies.
At a second stage, Menem plans to make unions not only compete between themselves for the $2.5 billion-healthcare system but also with private medical plans.

The government argues that deregulation will lead unions to streamline and merge their health plans, providing a better service. Many of the union plans are deep in debt, and members have had to seek duplicate coverage in private schemes.
It hopes to cut down the number of union plans from 300 now to not more than 80 by the end of next year.

Health Minister Alberto Mazza said Tuesday the government will ensure that all Argentines get proper medical services and that union health plans that do not meet the standards will "automatically lose their status."

But the CGT argues that, for all their problems, union health plans are the only ones that can ensure health coverage to every worker and his spouse and children, regardless of his or her income, medical record and number of family members.

Left to pick and choose, medical plans, especially private ones, will only take the top third of the wage pyramid and leave millions of workers with no coverage, CGT spokesman Carlos West Ocampo contended Tuesday.
Daer, buoyed by two successful strikes against Menem's austerity policies and labor flexibilization plans in August and September, said the time for dialogue was over.
"The one big dialogue was at the Plaza de Mayo," he said in reference to the workers' protest outside the government house after last month's 36-hour general strike.
Menem says that both health care deregulation and more flexible and modern labor legislation would improve the lot of Argentine workers and help combat 17 percent unemployment.
"Those are lies," Daer said. "They want to take us back to the turn of the century."
